3.2.1:
Why this matters

You almost never measure everything. You measure a sample, then draw conclusions about the whole process. Inference is how you do that honestly: it says not just "our best guess is 42 minutes", but "we are 95% confident the true average is between 39 and 45 minutes". Every hypothesis test in Analyze rests on this idea.

The big idea

Inference means using a sample to draw conclusions about a population (2.2.1). Because a sample is only part of the population, its results include sampling error: a different sample would give slightly different numbers. Inference measures that uncertainty.

There are two kinds of estimate:

  • Point estimate: a single best guess. The sample mean x̄ = 42 minutes is a point estimate of the population mean μ.
  • Interval estimate (confidence interval): a range likely to contain the true value. "39 to 45 minutes, with 95% confidence."

A point estimate alone hides how uncertain it is. An interval shows it.

Standard error

The standard error (SE) of the mean is the typical amount a sample mean varies from sample to sample:

SE = s ÷ √n

It is smaller than the standard deviation of individual values, and it shrinks as the sample grows: averages are more stable than individual readings. Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error.

Confidence interval for a mean

x̄ ± t(α/2, n − 1) × s ÷ √n
  • x̄: sample mean.
  • s ÷ √n: the standard error.
  • t: a multiplier from the t table, based on the confidence level and the degrees of freedom (df = n − 1).
  • The ± part is called the margin of error.

Worked example. 16 loads have an average unload time of 42 minutes, s = 6 minutes. Build a 95% confidence interval.

  1. SE = 6 ÷ √16 = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5.
  2. df = 15. For 95% two-sided, t(0.025, 15) = 2.131 (from the t table).
  3. Margin = 2.131 × 1.5 = 3.20.
  4. CI = 42 ± 3.20 = 38.8 to 45.2 minutes.

z or t?

  • If the population σ is known (rare), use the z multiplier: 1.96 for 95%, 2.576 for 99%, 1.645 for 90%.
  • If σ is estimated from the sample (s), use t. The t multiplier is larger than z for small samples, which widens the interval to account for the extra uncertainty of estimating σ. For large n, t approaches z.

Degrees of freedom

Degrees of freedom (df) count how many independent pieces of information remain to estimate variation. For a single sample's standard deviation, df = n − 1: once you know the mean, only n − 1 values are free to vary (the last one is fixed by the mean). Small df means heavier-tailed t distributions and larger multipliers.

What changes the width

ChangeEffect on the interval
Larger sample size nNarrower (SE falls)
Higher confidence level (99% instead of 95%)Wider
More variation (larger s)Wider

The only way to get a narrower interval and keep the same confidence is a larger sample (or less variation).

What "95% confident" really means

A 95% confidence interval comes from a method that, if repeated on many samples, would capture the true mean in about 95% of them.

Each sample gives a different interval. About 95 out of 100 such intervals contain the true mean.

It does not mean "there is a 95% probability the true mean is inside this particular interval". The true mean is fixed; this particular interval either contains it or not. The 95% describes the long-run success rate of the method.

Confidence interval for a proportion

p̂ ± z × √[ p̂(1 − p̂) ÷ n ]

Example: 24 of 200 shipments were late, p̂ = 0.12. SE = √(0.12 × 0.88 ÷ 200) ≈ 0.023. 95% CI = 0.12 ± 1.96 × 0.023 = 0.12 ± 0.045, about 7.5% to 16.5%.

Reading the IASSC t tables

The reference document has two t tables:

  • Table 1 columns are cumulative probabilities from 0.600 to 0.995 (headed "Alpha Risk", but the numbers are actually 1 − α). For a two-sided 95% interval or test at α = 0.05, use the 0.975 column.
  • Table 2 columns are one-tail α from 0.25 to 0.005, with more decimals. For two-sided α = 0.05, use 0.025; for one-sided α = 0.05, use 0.05.
  • Rows are df = n − 1 from 1 to 30, then 40, 60, 120 and ∞. For a df not listed, use the next lower listed df (more conservative).

Check your own copy, since table layouts vary between versions.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • To narrow an interval, increase n.
  • SE = s ÷ √n, not s.
  • The 95% describes the method, not one interval.
  • t when σ is estimated; z when σ is known.
  • Two-sided 95% uses α/2 = 0.025 in each tail (the 0.975 column).

Check yourself

  1. n = 25, x̄ = 80, s = 10. What is the standard error?
  2. Using t = 2.064 (df 24, 95%), what is the 95% confidence interval?
  3. What happens to the interval if you use 99% confidence instead?
  4. Your boss says "so there is a 95% chance the true mean is in this interval." What is the more accurate statement?
  5. 30 of 150 calls were abandoned. What is the 95% confidence interval for the abandonment rate?
Show answers
  1. 10 ÷ √25 = 2.
  2. 80 ± 2.064 × 2 = 80 ± 4.13, about 75.9 to 84.1.
  3. It gets wider.
  4. The method used to build it captures the true mean in 95% of samples; this interval either contains it or does not.
  5. p̂ = 0.20; SE = √(0.2 × 0.8 ÷ 150) ≈ 0.0327; 0.20 ± 0.064, about 13.6% to 26.4%.

Key takeaways

  • Inference: from sample to population, with measured uncertainty.
  • Point estimate vs interval estimate.
  • SE = s ÷ √n; CI for a mean = x̄ ± t × SE; for a proportion = p̂ ± z√[p̂(1 − p̂) ÷ n].
  • Wider with more confidence or more variation; narrower with larger n.
  • Use t when σ is estimated; df = n − 1.
3.2.2:
Why this matters

A sample is only useful if it represents the population. A biased sample gives confident-looking but wrong answers. And a sample that is too small cannot detect the differences you care about. This topic covers how to choose a sample and how big it needs to be.

Sampling methods

Probability methods (every item has a known chance of selection):

  • Simple random sampling: every item has an equal chance; for example, random numbers pick which loads to audit. The gold standard when the population is uniform.
  • Stratified sampling: divide the population into distinct subgroups (strata) such as terminals, shifts or customer types, then sample randomly within each. Ensures every subgroup is represented; ideal when subgroups differ.
  • Systematic sampling: take every kth item (every 10th invoice) after a random start. Simple and spreads the sample over time. Danger: if the process has a cycle that matches k, the sample can be badly biased.
  • Cluster sampling: divide the population into clusters (for example, days or trailers), randomly pick a few clusters, and measure everything in them. Cheaper when travel or access is costly, but less precise if clusters differ.

Non-probability methods (higher risk of bias):

  • Convenience sampling: whatever is easiest to get (the loads at the nearest dock). Quick, but often biased.
  • Judgment sampling: an expert picks "typical" items. Useful for exploration, but depends on the expert's assumptions.

Sampling bias

  • Selection bias: the method favors some items (only sampling day shift).
  • Non-response bias: in surveys, those who answer differ from those who do not (unhappy customers are more likely to respond, or less).
  • Undercoverage: some parts of the population are left out entirely (no data from the smallest terminals).

Random selection guards against these; a larger sample does not fix a biased method.

Sample size for estimating a mean

To estimate a mean within a margin of error E at a given confidence:

n = (Z(α/2) × σ ÷ E)²

Example: σ ≈ 8 minutes, and you want the average within ±2 minutes at 95% (Z = 1.96). n = (1.96 × 8 ÷ 2)² = (7.84)² ≈ 61.5, round up to 62.

Always round up, never down.

Sample size for estimating a proportion

n = Z² × p(1 − p) ÷ E²

Example: you expect about 10% late, and want the estimate within ±2 percentage points at 95%. n = 1.96² × 0.1 × 0.9 ÷ 0.02² = 3.8416 × 0.09 ÷ 0.0004 ≈ 864.4, round up to 865.

If you have no idea of p, use p = 0.5, which gives the largest (safest) n.

Notice proportions need much larger samples than means: discrete data carries less information (2.2.1).

Sample size for a hypothesis test (power)

Estimating a value needs precision (a margin of error). Testing for a difference needs power: the chance of detecting a real difference of a given size (3.3.3). The inputs are:

  • α: the false-alarm risk you accept (usually 0.05).
  • Power (1 − β): the chance of detecting a real difference (usually 0.80 to 0.90).
  • σ: the variation.
  • δ (delta): the smallest difference worth detecting.

Approximate formulas:

1-sample t: n ≈ (Z(α/2) + Z(β))² × σ² ÷ δ²
2-sample t (each group): n ≈ 2 × (Z(α/2) + Z(β))² × σ² ÷ δ²

Example: σ = 10, detect a 5-unit difference from a target, α = 0.05 (Z = 1.96), power 0.80 (Z(β) = 0.84). n ≈ (2.80)² × 100 ÷ 25 ≈ 31.4, about 32. For comparing two groups, about 63 per group.

n rises with more variation and more power; it falls with a bigger difference to detect or a larger α. Software (such as Minitab's power and sample size tool) does this calculation exactly.

Worked example: which method?

  1. "Audit every 25th bill of lading." Systematic.
  2. "Pick 10 random loads from each of the 6 terminals." Stratified.
  3. "Randomly choose 4 days and inspect every trailer those days." Cluster.
  4. "The supervisor picks the loads he thinks are typical." Judgment.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Every kth item = systematic. Random within subgroups = stratified. All items in chosen groups = cluster.
  • Round sample sizes up.
  • A bigger sample does not fix a biased method.
  • Estimation needs precision (E); testing needs power (α, power, σ, δ).

Check yourself

  1. Which method ensures each shift is represented?
  2. σ = 12, desired margin E = 3, 95% confidence. What sample size?
  3. No idea of the defect rate; want ±5 percentage points at 95%. What sample size?
  4. What four inputs determine sample size for a hypothesis test?
  5. Why can systematic sampling be risky?
Show answers
  1. Stratified sampling.
  2. (1.96 × 12 ÷ 3)² = (7.84)² ≈ 61.5, so 62.
  3. 1.96² × 0.25 ÷ 0.0025 ≈ 384.2, so 385.
  4. α, power (or β), σ, and the smallest difference worth detecting (δ).
  5. If the process has a repeating pattern that lines up with the sampling interval, the sample will be biased.

Key takeaways

  • Probability methods: random, stratified, systematic (every kth), cluster. Non-probability: convenience, judgment.
  • Avoid selection bias, non-response and undercoverage.
  • n for a mean = (Zσ ÷ E)²; for a proportion = Z²p(1 − p) ÷ E²; use p = 0.5 if unknown; round up.
  • Test sample size depends on α, power, σ and δ.
3.2.3:
Why this matters

The central limit theorem (CLT) is the reason so much of statistics works even when data are not normal. It explains why averages behave so predictably, why Xbar control charts work, and why t-tests hold up with moderately non-normal data.

The big idea

Take many samples of size n from any population, compute each sample's average, and look at how those averages are distributed. The CLT says:

  1. The averages center on the population mean μ.
  2. Their spread is the standard error σ ÷ √n, smaller than the spread of individual values.
  3. As n grows, their distribution becomes approximately normal, whatever the shape of the original population.

Even from a heavily skewed population, averages of just 10 values pile up in a narrow, nearly normal hump. Larger samples make it narrower and more normal still.

Why? Averaging cancels out extremes: a very high value in a sample tends to be balanced by others. The more values averaged, the more the extremes cancel.

How large must n be?

The often-quoted "n ≥ 30" is a classroom rule of thumb, not a law:

  • From a roughly symmetric population, averages look normal with n as small as 5 to 10.
  • From a strongly skewed or heavy-tailed population (or one with outliers), you may need much more than 30.

What the CLT does and does not do

  • It does make the distribution of sample means approximately normal.
  • It does not make the individual values normal. A skewed process stays skewed; only the averages are normal. Capability for individual parts (2.4) still needs to account for the real shape.

Why it matters in practice

  • Xbar charts (5.2) plot subgroup averages, so their limits work well even when individual values are somewhat non-normal.
  • t-tests and confidence intervals for means rely on the sampling distribution of x̄ being roughly normal, which the CLT supports for reasonable sample sizes.

Calculating with sample means

Because x̄ is approximately normal with mean μ and standard error σ ÷ √n, you can use z:

z = (x̄ − μ) ÷ (σ ÷ √n)

Example: load times have μ = 50 minutes, σ = 10 minutes. For samples of n = 25 loads:

  1. SE = 10 ÷ √25 = 2.
  2. Probability a sample average exceeds 54: z = (54 − 50) ÷ 2 = 2; P = 1 − 0.9772 = 0.0228.

Compare: the probability that a single load exceeds 54 is z = (54 − 50) ÷ 10 = 0.4, P ≈ 0.34. Averages rarely stray far; individual values often do.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Using σ instead of the standard error for questions about a sample mean. σ = 10 and n = 25 give SE = 2.
  • Believing the CLT makes individual data normal. Only averages.
  • Treating n ≥ 30 as a guarantee. It depends on the population's shape.

Check yourself

  1. What are the mean and standard error of sample averages of size n?
  2. σ = 12 and n = 36. What is the standard error?
  3. True or false: by the CLT, individual delivery times become normal with enough data.
  4. μ = 200, σ = 20, n = 16. What is the probability a sample mean is below 190? (Area left of z = −2 is 0.0228.)
  5. Why do Xbar charts tolerate non-normal individual data?
Show answers
  1. Mean μ; standard error σ ÷ √n.
  2. 12 ÷ 6 = 2.
  3. False. Only the distribution of averages becomes approximately normal.
  4. SE = 20 ÷ 4 = 5; z = (190 − 200) ÷ 5 = −2; probability ≈ 0.0228.
  5. Because they plot subgroup averages, which the CLT makes approximately normal.

Key takeaways

  • Sample means center on μ with spread σ ÷ √n and become approximately normal as n grows, whatever the population shape.
  • n ≥ 30 is only a rule of thumb; skewed data need more.
  • The CLT does not make individual values normal.
  • It is why Xbar charts and t-tests work well in practice.
